stimulus.text:
“Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.”

—First Amendment to the Constitution, proposed September 25, 1789, ratified December 15, 1791
stimulus.source_note: First Amendment to the Constitution, proposed September 25, 1789, ratified December 15, 1791. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — First Amendment to the Constitution, proposed September 25, 1789, ratified December 15, 1791, public domain.

primary_sources: First Amendment to the Constitution (proposed September 25, 1789; ratified December 15, 1791)

stem: According to the passage, which of the following laws would violate the First Amendment?

options.text: A law letting each state set its own rules for public schools
options.misconception: The passage limits what Congress may do, and school rules are not among the freedoms it lists.

options.text: A law requiring every citizen to serve on a jury when called
options.misconception: Jury service is not one of the freedoms the passage protects.

options.text: A law closing a public park at night to all visitors
options.misconception: Closing a park at night limits no listed freedom on its own terms.

options.text: A law making one church the official church of the United States

rationales.D: The passage forbids Congress to make a law “respecting an establishment of religion,” and an official church is exactly that.
rationales.A: The passage restricts Congress and lists five freedoms; state school rules touch none of them.
rationales.B: Jury service is a duty the passage never mentions, so requiring it breaks no listed freedom.
rationales.C: A night closing of a park, applied to everyone, touches no freedom the passage names.
rationales.general:
1. The passage lists five freedoms Congress may not take away: religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition.
2. An official church would be a law “respecting an establishment of religion,” the first freedom named.
3. School rules, jury service, and a park closing touch none of the five freedoms.
4. So only the official church breaks the passage as written.
Remember: test a law against the five freedoms the amendment actually names.
